clinicalPearls: Consider renal coloboma syndrome whenever optic disc anomalies, particularly the 'morning glory' disc or an optic disc coloboma, coexist with renal hypoplasia or dysplasia and otherwise unexplained chronic kidney disease.
Inheritance is autosomal dominant with striking variable expressivity, so a mildly affected parent may show only subtle optic disc changes while their child has significant renal failure.

Renal hypodysplasia, often with oligomeganephronia, drives the progressive kidney disease and makes this one of the important monogenic causes of chronic and end-stage renal disease presenting in childhood.
The optic disc anomaly is frequently asymptomatic or causes only mild visual deficit, so it must be actively sought with dilated fundoscopy rather than assumed absent.
Vesicoureteric reflux and recurrent urinary tract infection can be presenting features and may compound renal damage.
High-frequency sensorineural hearing loss is a recognised, though less consistent, association.
The same gene is implicated in some cases of isolated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and adult-onset chronic kidney disease occurring without any eye findings.
The disc lesion should be distinguished from glaucomatous cupping and from the colobomas seen in CHARGE syndrome and isolated ocular coloboma.
reference.pathophysiology: Renal coloboma syndrome, also termed papillorenal syndrome, is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in PAX2, a paired-box transcription factor essential for the development of the kidney, ureter, optic nerve and otic vesicle. PAX2 is expressed in the developing metanephric mesenchyme and Wolffian duct and in the optic stalk, where it participates in nephron induction and in closure of the optic (choroidal) fissure. Haploinsufficiency impairs these programmes, producing renal hypoplasia and dysplasia, classically small hypodysplastic kidneys with oligomeganephronia that progress to chronic kidney disease, together with an optic nerve dysplasia manifesting as the morning glory disc anomaly or optic disc coloboma, often accompanied by abnormal retinal vasculature. Vesicoureteric reflux, high-frequency hearing loss and, less commonly, central nervous system anomalies may also occur, and the phenotype shows marked variability in severity even within a single family.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT)
Isolated optic nerve coloboma or morning glory disc anomaly
Alagille syndrome, which may show both ocular and renal features
Isolated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis or familial chronic kidney disease
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasound to demonstrate small or hypodysplastic kidneys and oligomeganephronia
Serum creatinine with estimated glomerular filtration rate, and urinalysis for proteinuria
Dilated fundoscopy and formal ophthalmological assessment for optic disc coloboma or morning glory anomaly
Micturating cystourethrogram where vesicoureteric reflux is suspected
Audiometry for high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss
PAX2 genetic testing, with a broader CAKUT or HNF1B gene panel where the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Rapidly declining renal function or progression toward end-stage renal disease
Recurrent febrile urinary tract infection with reflux nephropathy
Significant visual impairment or retinal detachment associated with the disc anomaly
New or worsening proteinuria signalling glomerular involvement
reference.prognosis: The outlook is variable: many patients progress to chronic kidney disease and a substantial proportion reach end-stage renal disease during childhood or early adulthood, whereas the ocular anomaly is usually static and visual outcome ranges from normal to moderately impaired.
pitfalls: Diagnosing 'isolated' chronic kidney disease or renal hypoplasia without examining the optic discs, and thereby missing the unifying diagnosis.
Mistaking the optic disc coloboma or morning glory anomaly for glaucomatous cupping.
Not screening at-risk relatives because mild expressivity conceals the condition.
Overlooking vesicoureteric reflux as a modifiable contributor to renal damage.
references: Reviews of congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract
